UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT.
Fifteen Thousand Dollars Paid to Witnesses-A Negro Fiend Lynched in Russell County.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]
ABINGDON, VA., August 5, 1890.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

ABINGDON, VA., August 5, 1890.

The special term of the United States Court which has been in session since the 23d ultimo adjourned to-day. The grand jurors were dismissed and returned to their homes Saturday. More than a thousand witnesses have been paid off. They average about $15 each. Two hundred and eighty-six indictments were found, most of them being for the illegal traffic in whiskey.

A MAIL-ROBBERY CASE.

The most interesting case was that of Stephen B. Alley and Clabe Higgins, of Carroll county, charged with robbing the mail. The latter, a boy about sixteen years old, was mail-carrier, and the former was a justice of the peace for Carroll county, aged sixty-four years, and the husband of the postmaster, Mrs. Alley. Higgins confessed to the indictment, but swore he was instigated by Alley, who also furnished him the key to the sack, and with whom he divided the spoils. There was $300 stolen from registered packages. The story was admirably told, but being unsupported by other evidence and denied by the accused, Alley was acquitted and Higgins sentenced to four years in the reform school of Maryland. A number of cases have been continued to the next term, October 28th. Judge Paul leaves for his home in Harrisonburg, Va., to-morrow.

A NEGRO LYNCHED.

News has just reached here of the lynching of a negro Saturday night in Russell county for assaulting a white woman. About 4 o'clock Saturday afternoon a dissolute and desperate negro—Henry Jessies—entered the yard of a respectable farmer, near Dickinsonville, where his two daughters were standing. Attempting to grasp one of them they both screamed and fled to a neighboring house some distance off. The negro then entered the house and brutally assaulted the mother, who was quite an old woman. After accomplishing his purpose he took to the wooded hills. A posse of a hundred men succeeded in capturing him that night. He was identified and then swung up to a tree and his body riddled with bullets. The negro had only recently returned from the penitentiary, where he had served a term for forgery. The entire community is still very much enraged over the action of this fiend.

GRADING THEIR LINE.

The Abingdon Coal and Iron Railroad Company have put an additional force of hands grading their line of railroad from this place to Damascus.

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

ROANOKE, VA., August 6.—Ex-Mayor J. H. Dunston returned to-day from Lumpkin county, Ga., where he was sent several days ago to inspect some gold properties for a Roanoke and English syndicate. He reports the find good, and a company will be formed for the purchase. The South, he says, is improving and building up faster than ever before.

Hon. N. H. Houston and family, of Martinsville, arrived in the city to-night. The judge is a candidate for Congress in the Fifth district subject to the Democratic nomination and will probably come in as a dark horse.

KNOWS THE LYNCHERS.

John Jones, the negro fiend who assaulted Mrs. J. W. Gibson near Russell Court-house and was hanged by a mob, has a brotner in this city who says he can spot the lynchers and threatens to make it lively for them.

Hinton Helper, the journalist who has been doing great work for Virginia and the South generally, was taken suddenly ill several days ago, but is now improving.

A HAPPY MARRIAGE.

Mr. W. B. Moss, book-keeper in the Norfolk and Western offices and lieutenant of the Roanoke Light Infantry, was married at 6 o'clock this evening to Miss Maggie Kent, daughter of the late Dr. Kent and one of the most popular and attractive young ladies in the city. The military company attended the church in a body and did honor to their fellow-member and officer. The ceremony was performed by Rev. Dr. Meade, of the Episcopal Church. The happy couple left on the 7:20 train over the Shenandoah road for their bridal tour.

THE GOVERNOR CONFIDENT.

Governor P. W. McKinney, who is summering at Blue Ridge Springs, was in the city a few hours to-day shaking hands with old acquaintances. In conversation with your correspondent the Governor expressed himself would carry the State overwhelmingly this fall, and that the enemy would be routed horse foot and dra-
The amended charter of the furnace company was filed in the Clerk's office today. The capital is increased from $10,000 to $20,000.

SUITABLE TIMBER.

No delegates have as yet been appointed for the Democratic convention to be held in this city. The chairman will soon call a meeting and select suitable timber.

SHOT BY HIS BROTHER-IN-LAW.

Thomas Morris, a young colored man, was shot near Taylor's Store, in Franklin county, last night by his brother-law, William Edwards. The affair grew out of some family trouble. The wounded man was carried to his home and is doing as well as could be expected. Edwards escaped.

THE ROANOKE AND SOUTHERN.

There is but little or no talk at present of the Roanoke and Southern railroad failing to bring its main line to this city. The right of way in the corporate limits will be purchased by a stock company and given to the road. Colonel F. S. Fires, president of the Virginia and North Carolina Construction Company, was in the city to-day, and says the road will be running to Martinsville by December 1st, and the contract for the Roanoke end of the line will be let by September 1st. The road will then be under fair headway for completion. A great boom in real estate is expected in this city when the work is commenced.

O'Ferrall, our present able, experienced and efficient representative in Congress, was complimented with a nomination for a fifth term in that branch of our national legislature by acclamation, an honor that bristled all over with evidence from his constituents of "well done thou good and faithful servant."

After prayer by Rev. Dr. Hyde, of Winchester, a temporary organization was effected by placing Judge J. T. Lovell, of Warren, in the chair, and appointing Mr. Riley of the Times and Mr. Ward of the News, of Winchester, and other editors present, secretaries, after which the several counties and cities each named a delegate to represent them on the committees on organization, on credentials, and on resolutions, when the convention took a recess for a half hour to enable the several committees to make their reports.

When the convention reassembled the temporary organization was made permanent, and the report of the committee on credentials was adopted. The committee on resolutions, through its chairman, Gen Rosser, submitted its declarations concerning public questions, which were unanimously adopted. We did not take a copy of them, and therefore cannot lay them before our readers until next week, but we believe the great body of the democrats of the district will heartily endorse them.

The chair then announced that nominations were in order, when Capt. J. P. Dorsey, a member of the Farmers Alliance of this county, placed before the convention the name of Col. Chas. T. O'Ferrall. Mr. R. E. Byrd, of Winchester, in earnest and laudatory remarks concerning the record in war and upon the floors of Congress of our representative, of whom he said Virginia never had a braver, an abler and truer knight to stand up for her defence, seconded the nomination. At the conclusion of Mr. Byrd's remarks a member of the Frederick county delegation moved that Col. O'Ferrall's nomination be made by acclamation, which was carried amid wild applause.

The chair was then asked to appoint a committee to wait upon the nominee and inform him of the action of the convention and invite his attendance, together with that of Hons. C. Lewis of Mississippi and C. F. Crisp of Georgia. In a short time the committee reported with these gentlemen, who were greeted with applause, when Col. O'Ferrall proceeded to address the convention.

He began by saying that he was deeply touched by the manner in which the convention had spoken its endorsement of his public record—that, coming as it did from such an assembly of intelligent faces as sat before him, he could not help feeling proud of the pledge it brought to him of the confidence his constituents continued to repose in him. Especially was he touched at the endorsement he received on this occasion and at this place, because it was in Frederick county that his eyes first opened to the light of the sun, and it was amid her hills and fields he received the first lessons of self-reliance that had helped him to walk the honored path he was now treading. The position of trust and honor he enjoyed before that meeting was not due alone to his individual struggles, but to the many warm friends he had made in the district he was permitted to represent, and to his efforts to reflect worthily Virginia character and interest on all occasions On the battle field and in the forum of legislation he ever remembered that he was a Virginian, and he always endeavored to preserve in its brightness and exaltation such a birthright. He then briefly referred to the issue that would be prominent in the coming canvass, and hoped every democrat would do his duty. There were some who might forget party ties, and lend encouragement to a sneaking and self-constituted candidate, but the great masses of the democratic party were true to their organization and principles, and will register their fidelity to the same at the coming November election. Such were the substance of Col. O'Ferrall's remarks, which were brief, as he said there were other gentlemen present who were advertised to speak and who the audience would like to hear.

Hon. Clark Lewis, a representative in Congress from Mississippi and a member of the Farmers Alliance of that State, was then introduced. He said that as his ancestors had resided in Virginia and more

his heart beat in unison with the political aspirations of that noble race which had led Virginia up the path of greatness, and which had contributed so largely of the seed of true liberty planted in our form of government. He was a member of the Farmers Alliance, and at the same time he was a democrat. The Alliance was not a political organization. While its members were not enjoined to vote for the candidates of any particular party, nevertheless they were not expected to vote ignorantly of the sentiments entertained by candidates relating to questions affecting agricultural interests. His investigation of the legislation and aims of parties led him to believe that the interests of the Alliance were being promoted by the democratic party. That party was aiming to distribute the burthens of taxation with equal justice to all, and as the Alliance was endeavoring to break down all forms of class legislation, he thought its members could march side by side with the democrats in this important and necessary undertaking. In the Southern States its members cannot afford to overlook the reign of disorder threatened therein by one of the great parties of today, and the liberties, peace, prosperity and safety of the people of those States were bound up in maintaining the supremacy of the Anglo-Saxon race.

Hon. C. F. Crisp, of Georgia, was next introduced. Col. O'Ferrall, in his remarks, having referred to Judge Crisp as doing his courting in Virginia and his marrying in Georgia, the Judge said he was called upon to expose an act of Col. O'Ferrall's—that while he (the judge) was engaged in fighting the battles of Virginia and the Southland he was captured, and during his incarceration in a Federal prison Col O'Ferrall had captured his sweetheart, but he wished this kept a profound secret. Concerning the war and the part he had taken in it he had no apologies to offer. The past, with its sorrows and trials and sacrifices, was written, and we had to deal with the present and future, He was glad to hear some one in the audience ask, how about the tariff? It showed that the people were giving attention to questions affecting their interests, and with knowledge and experience concerning these matters the democratic party would succeed in its efforts to reform abuses on these lines. He was not disposed to heap abuse upon his political opponents, but rather to help the people to a knowledge of their rights in our form of government and their duty to assert them. Two principles found their exponents in the two parties of the day. One claimed that the national government may absorb all power to the injury of State autonomy, and that it might interfere with the business of individuals and pass laws in the interest of classes. The other claimed that the States created the national government, that the latter could not exist without the former, and that the individual should be taught to rely upon his own talents and resources for his personal advancement and prosperity, and should be given the fullest liberty consistent with the rights of others for the exercise of them. For his part he believed that the national government should never undertake to do that which a State is able to perform, and that a State ought not to assume functions which individuals are capable of discharging. He believed in the old axiom, that those were best governed who were least governed. He then presented some strong illustrations of the inequalities of our tariff laws. Bad Wreck in Texas. SHERMAN, Tex., Aug. 8.—The Dallas passenger train collided with a work-train here this afternoon, both trains running at a high rate of speed. Fireman Clopton jumped from the work-train and was injured Engineer Blair remained at his post and was also severely hurt. He said he was to blame for the accident. The engines were demolished and baggage and passenger coaches damaged. Between the engine and tender was found the mangled form of Lee Hughes, fireman of the Dallas train. He has since died. Engineer George Blake's head was crushed and his limbs broken. He cannot recover. Conductor Frank Salter's leg and arm were broken. R. B. Smith, of Denison, and E. O. Jones. of Hempstead, were both bruised about the head. TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES.
Vice-president Morton and family spent the day with Senator Hale, at Ellsworth, Me., yesterday.

Mr. Walter Damrosch and his wife arrived from Europe, on the steamer Columbia, yesterday.

The postoffice authorities have offered a reward of $200 for the apprehension of George Harris, the railway mail clerk.

Will Johnson, a negro boy, robbed two houses in Opelika, Ala., and Thursday killed P. J. Moore, a merchant of Gold Hill, who was trying to arrest him.

John L. Sullivan and Peter Jackson have been offered $30,000 purses; $25,000 to the winner and $5,000 to the loser, for a finish fight at the Carnival Palace, in Ogden, Utah.

On Sept. 8 will begin the Interstate shoot, at Milwaukee, in which teams representing the militia organizations of Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin will participate.

At Chicago, Mrs. Bersna, living on One-hundred-and-twenty-seventh street, attempted to light her fire with kerosene. The can exploded, burning her and her little girl six months old. Both died in five hours.

John Jordan, a negro in jail at Frankfort, Ky., confessed the crime for which he was arrested, the assault upon a little girl, near Peak's Mill, on Tuesday. There are threats of lynching, and an extra guard has been placed.

Tucson, A. T., is cut off from the East by railroad washouts. There has been no train for five days. The break cannot be repaired before Sunday. The storm last night cut of the California trains. The damage to the Southern Pacific company is estimated at $150,000.

Suit was brought Thursday against the assignee of E. L. Harper, the bank-wrecker, by the Western National Bank of New York for recovery on its claim of $200,000. The bank holds four $50,000 notes executed by Gahr and indorsed by Harper. Each note was secured by collateral in the form of 400 shares of Fidelity stock.

The recent action of the New York Coffee Exchange in making all coffee except that from the Congo a good delivery on future contracts has resulted in the withdrawal of the two principal buyers from the option business. The houses which have taken this step are Wm. H. Crossman & Bro. and Siegfried Gruner & Co.

W. B. Forbes, superintendent of the Greenville and Carillon canals, died recently at Ottawa, Ont. The government, suspecting that his accounts were not all right, ordered an investigation. The evidence shows that by falsification and misappropriations he had defrauded the government out of $5,000 a year for the past ten years.

CONDENSED TELEGRAMS.
The dry kiln connected with Hall's stave factory at Dyersburg, Tenn., was burned on the 7th. By a strong effort the main factory was saved. Loss fully covered by insurance.

C. T. Webster, who was put in jail at Lonoke, Ark., about ten days ago for running an original package house, was released on bond on the 7th, Judge Martin having reduced the bonds to $1,000 in the aggregate.

The large steam engine in Ackerman Bros.' stave factory at Milan, Tenn., blew up on the 6th, tearing the factory roof off and the engine to pieces. Too much steam had been put on by an inexperienced engineer, and shutting off steam too quick caused the accident. No one was hurt. This is the second time this engine has blown up.

JOHN JORDAN, a negro in jail at Frankfort, Ky., on the 7th, confessed the crime for which he was arrested, the outrage of a little white girl near Peak's Mill, Ky. There are threats of lynching, and an extra guard has been placed.

A CABLEGRAM received at Louisville, Ky., on the 7th, announces the death at Carlsbad, Germany, of the wife of Theodore Harris, president of the Louisville Railroad.

THE Hon. J. W. Cutrer, who killed Editor Chew, left on the 7th for Manitou Springs, Col., where he will join his wife.

REV. W. R. DALE, formerly pastor of the Sixth Baptist Church of Atlanta, has been convicted of bigamy at Dallas, Ga.

REV. TELFAIR HODGSON has resigned the chancellorship of the University of the South at Sewanee, Tenn., and the Rev. Thomas F. Gallor has been elected to fill the vacancy. Dr. Hodgson will still remain at the university as dear of the theological department.

Rev. Henry Duncan, or Talladega, Ala., was cured of deafness on the 6th by being struck by lightning and badly shocked. Mr. Duncan is 80 years old and had been entirely deaf several years. He was sitting by a window when lightning struck a tree near by. He was knocked senseless by the shock and when he recovered could hear perfectly.

The Farmers' Alliance, of the Third Kansas District, nominated B. H. Clover for Congress. Mr. Clover is president of the State Alliance.

The Author of an Atrocious Crime Hanged From a Tree.
He Confessed the Crime, and a Trial Was Considered Unnecessary.
Seventeen Carloads of Beef Cattle Suddenly Converted Into Hash.
Vigilantes in Pursuit of the Slayer of a Missouri Octogenarian.
LEXINGTON, Mo., Aug. 29.—An atrocious murder, the escape of the murderer, his arrest, confession of the crime and subsequent lynching. These are the elements of a double tragedy that was enacted at Mayview, ten miles south of here, to-day. Sheriff Mitchell received a telegram from Mayview this morning stating that H. F. Parker, a merchant of that place, had been murdered. The sheriff and two deputies started for the scene of the crime. Upon their arrival they went directly to Parker's store, where a ghastly sight met their gaze. In a pool of blood, behind the counter on the floor, with the head nearly severed from the body, lay the body of the dead man. The motive for the crime was most likely money, for the cash drawer was rifled and an examination of the clothes of Parker, who was a widower and slept in a room back of the store, showed that the pockets had been turned inside out. Forty dollars in cash and a gold watch was found which would suggest that the murderer was frightened away before his object was accomplished. Parker's mother lives in Sharon, Pa., and has been informed by telegraph of the crime. Dr. McDonald arrived from Mayview this evening and stated that a negro named William Walters had been arrested by Constable Thomas Chinn, for the murder of Parker, had confessed his crime and was hanged from the branch of a tree by a mob.

SWIFT JUSTICE.
A Negro Murderer Given Five Minutes to Pray.
A Negro Murderer Given Five Minutes to Pray.

LEXINGTON, Mo., Aug. 29.—A horrible murder and lynching occurred at May View, ten miles south of here this morning. Captain E. E. Parker, a prominent citizen of the county, was awakened about daylight and requested to open his store. The murderer made a pretense of buying clothing, and when Parker's back was turned attacks him with a hatchet. Parker's head was cut to pieces. An hour later his remains were found, and when it became known that a negro was seen leaving the store some time, before, a vigorous pursuit was organized, and the negro, Wm. Walton, was captured. He confessed to the murder, which he committed for the purpose of robbery, but only secured $7. He was given five minutes to pray and then swung up.

CHASING THE ASSASSIN.

A negro was seen to leave the rear of the house at about the time the murder was supposed to have been committed. He was recognized as one Will Walters, in the employ of H. C. Shider, a famer, residing three miles northeast of the city. Some citizens went in search of him and found him at work about the farm as usual. On searching him blood was found upon his clothing, and on being charged with the murder he confessed the crime. He said he went to the store and aroused Mr. Parker between 4 and 5 o'clock this morning. Parker admitted him to the store, when Walters asked to look at some shirts. Just as they were put down on the counter he struck Mr. Parker with a corn knife and continued to hack him until he was dead. His purpose was to get money, but he became alarmed and returned home.

THE VILLIAN LYNCHED.

The posse returned in the evening to Mayview, bringing the corn knife, covered with blood, with which Parker had been murdered, and stated the affair as above reported. They did not produce the negro, but it is positively known that he was made away with by some means, whether hung or shot is not stated.

Late yesterday evening Dr. McDonald arrived here from Mayview and confirms the statement that Walkers was caught a few miles north of Mayview, confessed the murder and was hung by a mob.

TWO FOUL MURDERS!
TWO TERRIBLE CRIMES COMMITTED IN ONE DAY.
AN UNPARALLELED RECORD OF CRIME FOR LAFAYETTE CO.
E. F. PARKER'S MURDER QUICK- LY AVENGEDED.
The Murderers of A. S. Higgins
Still at Large.
The Stories of Both Murders in Detail.
The darkest page in the history of Lafayette county was the one turned last Friday. On that day two of the most atrocious murders ever committed within her borders occurred.

The deadly work of the day was begun just before daylight that morning, by William Waters, who butchered Mr. E. F. Parker, a merchant of Mayview, come the brutal murder of Mr. A. S. Higgins, one of Lafayette's oldest and most respected citizens, by a man named William Feltz and an accomplice.

A part of the story of the first named crime was related in these columns last week, but at the time of our going to press the whole truth had not been made known to the public. When about one-half of our papers had been printed the news came that Waters, who killed Mr. Parker, had been caught, hung, and in order that all our readers may get all the facts, we commence at the beginning of the horrible story.

At about 3:00 o'clock a.m., last Friday, Wm. Waters, a negro boy, aged a little over 17, according to plans conceived by him the day before, arose from a hay mow on the farm of Mr. Henry C. Sheil, where he was working, went down to the stable, stole out a horse and proceeded to the village of Mayview, some three miles distant. He hitched the horse near the depot at that place and proceeded on foot to the general merchandise store of Mr. E. F. Parker.

Parker was a widower, with no children, and as had been his custom for many years, was sleeping in a room in the rear of the store when Waters walked up to the store door and tried to awake him by rapping on and shaking the door. Being unsuccessful in his attempt to arouse Mr. Parker, Waters went around to the side of the house and tapped upon the bed upon which the window immediately over the bed upon which
the opportunity to strike did not present itself while Parker was getting the cigars and Waters deferred his bloody work until the merchant began displaying his stock of clothing.

Shirts were called for by Waters and a selection made, and Parker wrapped them up. Pants were then called for and after several pairs had been spread upon the counter the opportunity for Waters to strike presented itself, for Parker had turned to the shelying and Waters was immediately behind him. He raised his corn-knife and struck Parker in the top of the head, laying the scalp open for a space beginning at the top of the forehead and extending back about four inches, and penetrating the skull to the depth of about one-twelfth of an inch. Parker turned and cried out to his murderer for mercy, but the murderous work had been commenced and had to be ended.

Another blow was struck. This time the knife caught on a line which had been stretched across the room for the purpose of hanging goods for display, and was diverted from the place the murderer intended to strike, but one of the most ghastly of the many wounds was inflicted by this stroke. Mr. Parker then attempted to get away from his murderer by going toward the front window of the store and behind a large upright show case, but Waters jumped over the counter and rushed to his victim, who had by this time fallen to the floor, and began hacking him in the neck. The wounded man was struggling and grooming and the negro continued cutting him in the neck until all groans were hushed and his victim lay perfectly still. These last strokes, added to the ones made while the victim was standing, made the sight that met the eyes of those who saw the body before its removal from the place where found, one of the most ghastly ever witnessed. The poor man's head was nearly severed from his shoulders, and was left hanging thereon by only a few muscles and very little flesh.

He then began his search for money. One pocket in the murdered man's pants was turned inside out, but no money found therein. The other pocket which was on the side next to the floor and in the blood, contained $7 60 in silver, but was not molested. Waters then took his corn-knife and pried open the cash drawer, but found no money.

He then heard a noise without, picked up the bundle of shirts and a few other things, blew out the lamp and fled. He went directly to Mr. Sheir's farm, ate his breakfast, and, in company with the latter named gentleman came to a place near this city for two loads of corn.

Mr. Parker's store is on the main street of Mayview. About 100 yards east of the store is the home of J. P. Maw, where Parker ate his meals. At 6 o'clock Mr. Maw went to the store as was his wont to call Parker to break fast. He found the door locked, and thinking Parker was still asleep did not try to wake him. Half an hour later Maw returned and still found the store locked. He shook the door several times, but getting no answer went to the rear door opening into Parker's bedroom, intending to knock on that and so arouse him.

This rear door Maw found standing wide open and he stepped into the room. He found this disarranged and Parker's coat and vest hanging from the back of a chair. The door leading into the store was open and thinking Parker was in there Maw stepped to the connecting door to announce that breakfast was ready. The shutters in front being tightly closed the interior of the store was dark and Maw could see nothing. He lighted a match, and holding it over his head peered into the room. Still he could not see the store keeper, and he walked behind the counter in the west side of the store. There under the flickering blaze of his match the fearful sight met his gaze.

Stretched on the floor, his feet toward the front, lay Parker's body in a pool of blood. Stooping over the body and touching it Maw found it was still warm, but the wound showed, even to his excited mind, that life must be extinct.

Maw quickly gave the alarm and in fifteen minutes the little store and the street

On top of the show case on the counter immediately above the body lay several boxes of shirts and some tro users spread out just as the murdered man had laid them for the inspection of the dastard who struck him down.

The news of the tragedy spread rapidly for Parker was a popular man and a rapid and systematic investigation was begun for clews. The fact that the body was still warm pointed to a period about an hour or two previous as the time of the murder or about or just preceding daylight.

Inquiry was then made for any strangers who might have been seen in the streets of the village the night before and this method led to valuable developments. Alex Dyer, a colored man who lived back of Parker's store, stated that as he went to his back door, which opened in the alley, about 100 yards from the rear of Parker's store, he saw a negro dart across the alley back of the store and run in a northwesterly direction to the road leading to Lexington.

This evidence was speedily supplemented by that of Wm. Dyer, a brother, who had left the house some few minutes before his brother went to the back door. Will was going to a job of work some distance away and his road led him directly by the front of Parker's store. As he passed he noticed it was open and that a lighted lamp stood on the counter. By its light he saw Mr. Parker back of the counter reaching up to a shelf for something, while in front of the counter stood a young colored man he recognized as Will Waters. He thought at the time it was strange for Waters to be in town at such an early hour, but made no inquiry.

This much was learned by 9 o'clock, and a party of men, mounted and on foot, at once started for Shier's farm. They reached there in about half an hour, but neither Shier nor the negro hand was there. Mrs. Shier stated that they had gone to Lexington for corn, and the party started in that direction. After traveling about two miles they met Shier and the negro returning, each driving a wagon load of corn.

Waters was told that he was wanted for the murder of Parker, but he stoutly protested his innocence.

“What’s that blood on your hat and on your shirt,” and one of his accusers pointed to several bright red splashes on the front of his straw hat and in the bosom of his shirt just about the edge of his trousers.

“That’s where I had the nose bleed,” said the negro and he still manifested ignorance of the crime.

Shier was called on next and he told that Waters had not been in the house all night. He had some home early that morning on one of his horses and when he scolded him for it Waters said that he had been over to Mayview to get some clothes he had bought the night before.

The clothes were found in the barn at Shier’s farm by the party when they reached there and were part of the same lot that lay scattered about on top of the counter in the murdered man’s store and like them were also splashed with blood.

Still Waters protested his innocence, but everything pointed so strongly to his guilt that a halter was thrown over his head and he was swung up to the limb of a tree in the barnyard. The latter broke when his full weight came upon it and the negro fell a limp mass upon the ground. The driving lines were next detached from the harness of the team Waters had been driving and quickly fashioned into a noose and it was thrown over his head and the crowd were about to swing him up again.

Then Waters fell upon his knees and began bawling for mercy. “I killed him, I killed him,” he yelled, “but please don’t hang me, misters. I didn’t mean to do it, but I wanted to get—” and the wretch lay groveling in the dirt of the barnyard.

There was a strong disposition on the part of the crowd to hang him then and there, but cool counsel prevailed.

"What did you kill Mr. Parker with?" was asked.
"A corn knife," was the answer, and he led his captors to a clump of weeds about a quarter of a mile away and got the instrument of butchery.
The crowd started toward Mayview with it and their prisoner, but half way there they heard that officers from Lexington were waiting for them to take the prisoner.
A decision was quickly reached and the party divided, one-half going back to Mayview, taking the corn knife, and the other half with the prisoner cut across the fields in to a dense patch of wood a mile west of town and there lay until dark.
The party that went into town reported to the authorities that Waters had escaped them and had probably gone to Lexington, where his parents lived, and the officers went to Lexington.
Out in the patch of woods just off the Chicago and Alton track and in plain sight of the village, the captors and their prisoner spent the remainder of the day. The latter was bound hand and foot.
Long before nightfall a confession had been extracted from the wretch, who fully realized the fearful fate that was impending for him.
The confession, as it was afterward related by several of the captors, was as follows: "Yesterday, Thursday, I was at the Higginsville fair, I met Mr. Parker, He had a big roll of money and I felt like taking it away from him, but I would be caught. I thought I could do it better by waiting until morning when I could catch him in his store alone and knock him down. So I went home and slept in the hay mow in the barn. I guess it was about 3 o'clock when I woke up, for the moon was shining bright. I went down to the stable and bridled one of Shier's horses and started for Mayview.
In passing the corn field near the house I got off and went to a shock of corn where I had left my corn knife, then I rode on to Mayview. I hitched my horse to a tree just outside near the depot and went to Parker's store. I knocked but nobody answered and I walked around to the back and knocked on the window. Mr. Parker said 'Who's there?' and I said, 'Bill Waters.' 'What do you want, Will,' said he and I says. 'Want to get some shirts, Mr. Parker.' 'All right, just walk around to the front and I'll get up and let you in.' So I walks around and pretty soon he opened the door and says, 'Ain't you a little bit early, Will?' I says 'Yes, sir, I am, but I wanted some shirts so that I could go to the fair.' 'What are you doing with that corn knife?' says he, pointing to the knife. william-walters-lexington-1890-08-29.A26:
The murder of "uncle" A. S. HIGGINS.

While the people throughout the county were anxiously inquiring for news of the Mayview murder, they were horrified to hear of another murder, that of "Uncle" A. S. Higgins, one of the pioneer citizens of Lafayette county, at the Vivlon House, in Higginsville, by a man named Wm. Feltz.

Feltz had been an employee at Dooley & Son's livery stable since about April 1, most of the time working inside the stable. During the press of business, brought about by the fair, Feltz was put to driving a carriage to and from the fair grounds. Friday afternoon he drove up to the ticket office at the grounds and purchased tickets for two ladies whom he had brought out and when he drove through the gate he refused to give to the gate keeper the two tickets. Mr. Higgins was the head gate-keeper and the fact that Feltz refused to give up the tickets was reported to him. Mr. Higgins promptly sent a policeman after Feltz and the tickets were secured. When Feltz came down to the gate he met Mr. Higgins and a heated conversation took place in which Feltz called Higgins a d-d liar. Mr. Higgins was a man about 75 years of age, but he was active and strong and did not hesitate to proceed to chastise Feltz for calling him such a name. He raised his walking stick and knocked Feltz down. Bystanders interfered and Feltz was ejected from the grounds. After he had driven down the road a little way he met Mr. Harvey Dooley, the junior member of the firm for whom he was working. Feltz related his story to him and Mr. Dooley thought he deserved being discharged, and did discharge him, telling him to report at the stable the next morning, and if he was found not to be in the wrong he would be reinstated in his position.

His anger thoroughly aroused by the above related occurrences, Feltz began preparations to get revenge, and from what followed it seems that he planned well.

Uncle "As." was and had been for several years boarding at the Vivlon House, just southwest of the Missouri Pacific depot, and when Feltz thought it was time he had gone to supper he went around to the hotel and made inquiries for him. Mr. Higgins had not come when Feltz made inquiry for him and he left the hotel and went back up town. Shortly afterward someone at the hotel was taken sick and Mr. Geo. Vivion went for a doctor. As he was emerging from the doctor's office he noticed Feltz talking to two other men and heard one of them remark. "We'll get him." After a short period of time had elapsed after Mr. Vivion had returned from the doctor's office, Feltz and another man (who is supposed to be a brother) came back and inquired for Mr. Higgins, who was at the time eating his supper. Mr. Vivion went into the dining room and told Mr. Higgins that a man who looked as if he was quite angry was outside looking for him. As soon as Mr. Higgins finished his supper he walked out into the hotel office and saw the man with whom he had had the fuss standing just outside. The man motioned to him and asked him to come out of the hotel. Mr. Higgins replied that he did not wish to have any trouble with him and that he was not going to leave the hotel. He then left the office and went to his room, returning shortly afterward with a double-barrelled shot gun. When he appeared with the shot gun, one of the men stepped to the side of the door, on the outside, and the other one inquired of Mr. Higgins, "What are you going to do with that gun?" Mr. Higgins replied to the effect that he was going to defend himself. As soon as he said this the man at the side of the door made a grab, caught hold of the gun and wrenched it from Mr. Higgins, at the same time pulling him out of the house into the street. Mr. George Vivion then grappled with the man who had taken charge of the gun and the man who had been urging Mr. Higgins to go outside the hotel grappled with Mr. Higgins.

Mr. Vivion showed great presence of mind and was very active for a man of his age. He retained a hold on the shot gun and while the scuffle for the possession of it was in progress he cocked one barrel of it at a time and when the opportunity presented itself fired both loads into the air.

While this scuffle was in progress Mr. Higgins was faring badly. His assailant had a huge knife and was cutting him in a fearful manner. He had struck him with the knife first in the right ear, and felled him to the ground. He then pounced onto him and began stabbing him in various places. When the knife struck Mr. Higgins in the ear it ranged downward and to the front, severing both carotated arteries and the jugular vein. With the assistance of a bystander, Mr. Higgins regained his feet, but Feltz's murderous assaults were renewed. Mr. G. Chamblin rushed between Mr. Higgins and his assailant, but was knocked down on his hands and knees by the latter striking him in the back of the head with his first. Feltz then made another vicious cut at his victim and his bloody work was ended. The knife this time struck Mr. Higgins in the breast, near the right shoulder and ranged toward the breast bone.
